skills.name: fix-slow-queries
skills.desc: Diagnose and fix slow Paperclip PostgreSQL queries using Cloud and Neon evidence, local reproduction, performance and result comparisons, regression tests, and a PR with passing checks. Use for costly queries, repeated database work, or slow requests with a suspected database cause.
skills.body:
---
name: fix-slow-queries
description: >-
  Diagnose and fix slow Paperclip PostgreSQL queries using Cloud and Neon evidence,
  local reproduction, performance and result comparisons, regression tests, and
  a PR with passing checks. Use for costly queries, repeated database work, or
  slow requests with a suspected database cause.
---

# Fix Slow Queries

Deliver a measured improvement with preserved behavior and a reviewable PR whose
latest commit passes checks. A list of suspicious SQL or an unverified rewrite
is an intermediate result. Respect a narrower request for diagnosis only.

## 1. Establish the target and finish line

- Resolve the reported URL, environment, company/workspace, deployed revision,
  owning repository, and local checkout. Read its `AGENTS.md` and scoped rules.
  Paperclip and the private `paperclip-cloud` control plane have different rules.
- Work in a dedicated branch/worktree. Reuse suitable existing work; keep the
  checkout running a live server out of branch switching and benchmark setup.
- Select a bounded batch, usually the top two or three query families. Record
  deferred candidates so discovery does not turn into an unbounded rewrite.
- The finish line is: reproducible baseline, faster treatment, output/behavior
  proof, relevant regression coverage, and green checks on each final PR head.
  A concrete access or infrastructure blocker must be reported as incomplete.

## 2. Find the actual database and rank the work

Read [Cloud discovery](references/cloud-discovery.md) when starting from a hosted
workspace. Follow the chain from Paperclip Cloud fleet admin to the stack's Neon
project, branch, endpoint, database, and runtime role. Record the corresponding
application deployment and time window. Do not reuse IDs from a previous run.

Capture query text/fingerprint, calls, total execution time, mean time, rows,
and available I/O, temporary-file, and lock-wait evidence. Rank both expensive
individual calls and frequent work with high aggregate cost. Group variants by
their actual caller; do not add unrelated query means into an endpoint latency.

Keep three claims separate:

| Claim | Evidence needed |
| --- | --- |
| SQL is expensive | Query statistics and a reproducible execution plan |
| The database path dominates a slow request | Correlated SQL, connection wait, and application timings |
| More database capacity would help | Resource/queue pressure in the same window and a capacity-specific experiment |

Cumulative query statistics are not a recent-window trace. Capture reset times
or two snapshots and calculate deltas. A large database-time total alone does
not justify resizing Neon. Application CPU headroom also does not rule out a
busy Node main thread.

## 3. Trace each candidate to its behavior

Use `rg` on distinctive SQL fragments, table names, JSON keys, and predicates.
Trace the full path: route or scheduler → service → generated SQL → indexes.
Record frequency, fan-out, page limits, redaction, authorization, and any second
query the caller performs. Compare the deployed implementation with local code.

State a falsifiable cause and the contract the fix must preserve. Typical causes
include casts on indexed columns, repeated detoasting of large JSON, broad
candidate scans, unbounded result sets, duplicate reads, and unnecessary polling.
Use plans and caller evidence to choose among them.

Inspect existing indexes and recent related fixes before adding another index.
For advisory locks, identify the caller, key, transaction duration, and wait
chain first. Preserve checkout, leases, ownership, recovery, and no-replay rules;
removing a lock or polling loop is not a query optimization by itself.

## 4. Reproduce the baseline locally

Read [Local proof](references/local-proof.md) before building or changing the
benchmark. Use disposable real PostgreSQL and synthetic data with representative
row counts, selectivity, and payload sizes. Record the PostgreSQL version and
any difference from the hosted server.

Pin the pre-fix commit. Capture the complete SQL and parameters the real service
generates, including projections, joins, ordering, limits, and relevant imported
query helpers. Prove the baseline exhibits the suspected cost before editing.
If it does not, improve the fixture or revise the hypothesis.

Save baseline results, timings, and `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)`.
Define the performance acceptance criterion for this fixture before measuring
the treatment. Avoid a brittle universal millisecond threshold.

## 5. Implement and prove both kinds of green

Make the smallest change supported by the measurements. Author the fix on our
branch from source and evidence. Related community reports can supply leads;
respect any instruction to keep the implementation independent of their code.

Run baseline and treatment against equivalent fixtures under the same settings:

- **Performance:** use warmups and repeated samples, report medians and spread,
  and examine plan/buffer changes. Alternate order or repeat in reverse order
  when caching could explain the gain. Report neutral or slower paths honestly.
- **Correctness:** compare every returned SQL column and the externally visible
  behavior. Preserve ordering, duplicates, nulls, tenant scope, and redaction.
  A faster wrong result fails even when row counts match.

When intentionally bounding history, compare query speed at the same result
limit separately from the contract change. Test default/max limits and older
record access. Do not call truncated output equivalent to the former full list.

Reject or revise the change if either proof fails. Keep the reproducible harness
with the source where repository conventions allow it; keep bulky evidence out
of git. Exhaust viable query/caller changes and existing indexes before proposing
an exceptional migration. Document the serious reason and why migration-free
alternatives are insufficient. Do not add startup scripts, boot-time DDL, or
recurring backfills to bypass the migration constraint.

If a migration remains necessary, follow the database migration rules and the
production-size timing procedure in [Local proof](references/local-proof.md).
Measure the complete migration, including index builds, backfills, and lock waits.
First optimize a migration exceeding the roughly one-to-two-minute budget; if
it cannot be brought within an acceptable duration, flag it for human review
with the measured timings and alternatives before presenting it as deployable.

## 6. Verify the blast radius

Choose checks from the caller graph and affected contracts, not only the edited
function. Relevant cases from this workflow include:

| Change | Regression evidence |
| --- | --- |
| UUID/JSON joins | Canonical, uppercase, malformed, missing and non-string IDs; native/legacy precedence; company scope |
| JSON projections | Scalar/array/object/null inputs, text conversion, all fields, redaction |
| History bounds | Service and route callers, UI/API defaults, older deep links, empty recent history, retry and navigation races |
| Ownership/recovery reads | Retained processes, active leases, blocked replay, workspace failure, receipts and delivery |
| Polling/caching | Idle work reduction, committed-change wakes, missed events, restart/sleep recovery, fresh destructive checks |

Use real database tests for SQL semantics. Exercise assembled services/routes
and actual UI components when those are affected. Update query mocks when the
builder shape changes; a broken mock is not evidence that runtime SQL is wrong.

Run focused checks first, then the owning repository's required pre-PR checks.
For this repo, consult `AGENTS.md` for typecheck, full tests, build, and conditional
map/token/migration gates. Capture command, commit, exit status, and log location.
Do not call an interrupted suite a pass. Preserve its partial evidence and state
what completed locally versus on the final commit in CI.

## 7. Create the PR and carry it through checks

Use [prepare-paperclip-pr](../prepare-paperclip-pr/SKILL.md) for public Paperclip
changes, [check-pr](../check-pr/SKILL.md) for feedback, and
[prcheckloop](../prcheckloop/SKILL.md) for checks. Follow the owning repository's
workflow instead when the fix belongs in `paperclip-cloud`.

- Use the full PR template. Include cause, contract, benchmark command, baseline
  revision, fixture, before/after timings, equality evidence, regression results,
  and remaining risks. Label synthetic local timings as local SQL measurements.
  For an exceptional migration, include its justification, production-size fixture,
  complete duration, blocking time, optimization attempts, and any human decision
  still needed. Query speedup does not establish acceptable migration cost.
- Split independent fixes into independently reviewable PRs; disclose actual
  dependencies. Attach every created PR to the current chat/task where supported.
- After each push, refresh the head SHA. Address actionable reviews and failures,
  rerun affected local proof, and wait for fresh review and all expected checks
  on that SHA. Follow this repo's Greptile 5/5/no-unresolved-findings requirement.
- Distinguish code failures from runner shutdowns or external outages. Rerun a
  demonstrated transient failure once. Cancel obsolete runs only after verifying
  they belong to this work and an older head; never terminate unrelated jobs.
- Do not finish with "CI pending." Continue the loop within its repair bounds,
  or report the exact blocker, check URL, attempts, and next action. An empty
  check list, an old review score, or a draft-only subset of checks is not green.

Thanking contributors and closing their PRs requires explicit authorization.
When authorized, explain which report our verified PR covers, acknowledge any
uncovered scope, and leave unrelated PRs open. This skill does not itself grant
permission to comment, close, merge, deploy, resize, or mutate a hosted database.

## Constraints

- your solution should not require a migration script to be run unless there is a serious reason - in almost all cases a migration script is a non starter
- similarly you should not add some new boot script - e.g. dont' work around migration scripts by running the migration on every boot
- if you add migrations, you should also have a sense on the time it will take on a large paperclip instance with thousands of tasks. the best option is to test on a clone of a production-size database and time it. if you don't have that you should make one. migrations that take an unacceptably large time to run (e.g. more than 1 or 2 minutes) must be flagged - first try to optimize the migration and then flag for a human if that's impossible

## 8. Hand off the evidence

Report each PR URL and final head, measured gains and neutral paths, correctness
comparison, completed local checks, latest-head CI/review status, and limitations.
If working from a Paperclip issue, attach evidence/work products using the
repository's artifact workflow. Keep private identifiers and tenant data out of
public PRs. State whether anything was deployed.

If rollout is authorized, verify the deployed revision and compare a fresh,
comparable query-statistics window and request timing. Until then, production
latency improvement remains unverified even when local SQL is much faster.

map/token/migration gates. Capture command, commit, exit status, and log location.
Do not call an interrupted suite a pass. Preserve its partial evidence and state
what completed locally versus on the final commit in CI.

## 7. Create the PR and carry it through checks

Use [prepare-paperclip-pr](../prepare-paperclip-pr/SKILL.md) for public Paperclip
changes, [check-pr](../check-pr/SKILL.md) for feedback, and
[prcheckloop](../prcheckloop/SKILL.md) for checks. Follow the owning repository's
workflow instead when the fix belongs in `paperclip-cloud`.

- Use the full PR template. Include cause, contract, benchmark command, baseline
  revision, fixture, before/after timings, equality evidence, regression results,
  and remaining risks. Label synthetic local timings as local SQL measurements.
  For an exceptional migration, include its justification, production-size fixture,
  complete duration, blocking time, optimization attempts, and any human decision
  still needed. Query speedup does not establish acceptable migration cost.
- Split independent fixes into independently reviewable PRs; disclose actual
  dependencies. Attach every created PR to the current chat/task where supported.
- After each push, refresh the head SHA. Address actionable reviews and failures,
  rerun affected local proof, and wait for fresh review and all expected checks
  on that SHA. Follow this repo's Greptile 5/5/no-unresolved-findings requirement.
- Distinguish code failures from runner shutdowns or external outages. Rerun a
  demonstrated transient failure once. Cancel obsolete runs only after verifying
  they belong to this work and an older head; never terminate unrelated jobs.
- Do not finish with "CI pending." Continue the loop within its repair bounds,
  or report the exact blocker, check URL, attempts, and next action. An empty
  check list, an old review score, or a draft-only subset of checks is not green.

Thanking contributors and closing their PRs requires explicit authorization.
When authorized, explain which report our verified PR covers, acknowledge any
uncovered scope, and leave unrelated PRs open. This skill does not itself grant
permission to comment, close, merge, deploy, resize, or mutate a hosted database.

## Constraints

- your solution should not require a migration script to be run unless there is a serious reason - in almost all cases a migration script is a non starter
- similarly you should not add some new boot script - e.g. dont' work around migration scripts by running the migration on every boot
- if you add migrations, you should also have a sense on the time it will take on a large paperclip instance with thousands of tasks. the best option is to test on a clone of a production-size database and time it. if you don't have that you should make one. migrations that take an unacceptably large time to run (e.g. more than 1 or 2 minutes) must be flagged - first try to optimize the migration and then flag for a human if that's impossible

## 8. Hand off the evidence

Report each PR URL and final head, measured gains and neutral paths, correctness
comparison, completed local checks, latest-head CI/review status, and limitations.
If working from a Paperclip issue, attach evidence/work products using the
repository's artifact workflow. Keep private identifiers and tenant data out of
public PRs. State whether anything was deployed.

If rollout is authorized, verify the deployed revision and compare a fresh,
comparable query-statistics window and request timing. Until then, production
latency improvement remains unverified even when local SQL is much faster.

skills.name: garden-inbox
skills.desc: Scan a Paperclip user's Mine inbox, classify reversible archive candidates, request checkbox confirmation, and archive only accepted selections. Use when asked to garden, clean up, prune, or tidy a Paperclip inbox without changing issues, branches, or workspaces.
skills.body:
---
name: garden-inbox
description: Scan a Paperclip user's Mine inbox, classify reversible archive candidates, request checkbox confirmation, and archive only accepted selections. Use when asked to garden, clean up, prune, or tidy a Paperclip inbox without changing issues, branches, or workspaces.
---

# Garden Inbox

Use the bundled script for every stage. Keep the workflow strictly ordered: `scan` → `confirm` → `apply`.

## Safety contract

- Treat `scan` as read-only. It may read inbox, workspace, close-readiness, and local Git metadata only.
- Treat `confirm` as a confirmation-card write only. It must not archive inbox entries or mutate issue fields, branches, or workspaces.
- Run `apply` only after a resolved `request_checkbox_confirmation` interaction. It archives only accepted option IDs that also occur in the originating `candidates.json`.
- Remember that inbox archive state is per-user presentation state. It is reversible and does not change the underlying issue.
- Never substitute issue status changes, branch deletion, workspace cleanup, or issue deletion for inbox archiving.

## Inputs

Require `PAPERCLIP_API_URL` and `PAPERCLIP_API_KEY`. The script strips a trailing `/api` from the URL. It resolves the target user from the run JWT payload's `responsible_user_id`; use `--user-id <uuid>` only for an explicit target override.

Use a run-owned output directory when available:

```bash
RUN_DIR="${PAPERCLIP_RUN_SCRATCH_DIR:-${PAPERCLIP_TASK_SCRATCH_DIR:-.}}/garden-inbox"
mkdir -p "$RUN_DIR"
```

## 1. Scan

```bash
node .agents/skills/garden-inbox/scripts/garden-inbox.mjs scan \
  --output-dir "$RUN_DIR" \
  --stale-days 60
```

Inspect `garden-inbox-report.md` and `candidates.json`. The report groups every inbox row into exactly one bucket:

The scan reads Mine separately for each included issue status so the endpoint's global 500-row cap does not silently omit older rows. If any single-status query reaches that cap, both outputs mark coverage as possibly truncated; do not treat that scan as complete.

- A: merged/archived workspace and all linked work terminal; selected by default.
- B: terminal or workspace-gone work idle beyond the threshold; selected by default.
- C: stale work with commits ahead of base; never selected by default.
- D: keep; never offered for archiving.

Do not manually promote bucket D entries into the candidate file.

## 2. Confirm

Post checkbox interactions on the driving issue:

```bash
node .agents/skills/garden-inbox/scripts/garden-inbox.mjs confirm \
  --issue-id "$PAPERCLIP_TASK_ID" \
  --candidates "$RUN_DIR/candidates.json"
```

The script posts sequential cards when a scan has more than 200 candidates. Re-running `confirm` with the same scan file is idempotent. Leave the driving issue in the waiting posture required by the surrounding Paperclip heartbeat workflow.

When a candidate was declined by the user in an earlier pass, pass `--unselect <issueId>` (repeatable) so it starts unchecked and its description notes the earlier decline. Never re-offer previously declined items as default-checked.

For development or payload review, suppress the POST:

```bash
node .agents/skills/garden-inbox/scripts/garden-inbox.mjs confirm \
  --issue-id "$PAPERCLIP_TASK_ID" \
  --candidates "$RUN_DIR/candidates.json" \
  --dry-run
```

## 3. Apply accepted selections

After an interaction-resolution wake, take the resolved interaction ID from the wake payload and run:

```bash
node .agents/skills/garden-inbox/scripts/garden-inbox.mjs apply \
  --issue-id "$PAPERCLIP_TASK_ID" \
  --interaction-id "$INTERACTION_ID" \
  --candidates "$RUN_DIR/candidates.json"
```

On rejection, expiry, or an accepted empty selection, the script archives nothing. Apply preserves the scan file's target user, including an explicit `--user-id` override. Its summary includes the API undo path and target-user body for every archived row.

Test `apply` without API writes by supplying a saved interaction response:

```bash
node .agents/skills/garden-inbox/scripts/garden-inbox.mjs apply \
  --issue-id "$PAPERCLIP_TASK_ID" \
  --interaction-file resolved-interaction.json \
  --candidates "$RUN_DIR/candidates.json" \
  --dry-run
```

## Verify the bundled logic

Run the zero-dependency Node tests after changing classification or selection safety:

```bash
node --test .agents/skills/garden-inbox/scripts/garden-inbox.test.mjs
```

skills.name: honeycomb-tracing
skills.desc: Trace Paperclip runs, requests, and full CI suites in Honeycomb. Use to find traces, diagnose latency, design readable and foldable waterfalls, configure opt-in OpenTelemetry, or add missing spans.
skills.body:
---
name: honeycomb-tracing
description: >-
  Trace Paperclip runs, requests, and full CI suites in Honeycomb. Use to find
  traces, diagnose latency, design readable and foldable waterfalls, configure
  opt-in OpenTelemetry, or add missing spans.
---

# Honeycomb Tracing

Produce an inspectable waterfall tied to the actual run or CI attempt, explain
which intervals dominate elapsed time, and identify the smallest useful next
experiment. Respect diagnosis-only requests; tracing does not itself authorize
replaying tasks, changing credentials, or deploying instrumentation.

## Choose the data path

| Question | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Why is a task slow before, during, or after model execution? | Application workflow below; [runtime setup](references/runtime.md) if spans are absent |
| Why does an issue page load slowly? | Request spans plus browser timing, described below |
| Which CI jobs or test files delay the whole suite? | [CI profiling](references/ci.md) |
| How should a trace be organized so a person can understand it? | Human-readable waterfall guidance below and [trace design](references/trace-design.md) |
| Where should a new span go? | Instrumentation guidance below and [Observability contract](../../../doc/observability.md) |

Repository-relative paths and commands assume the checkout root. The maintained
contracts are `doc/observability.md` and `doc/ci-profiling.md`; recheck them and
the owning code when a deployed version differs.

Keep the repository's three paths distinct:

- **Observability:** operator-configured OpenTelemetry export to Honeycomb or
  another OTLP destination. With no endpoint, this tracing stays off.
- **Telemetry:** first-party events under `packages/shared/src/telemetry/`, sent
  to Paperclip by default unless opted out. Adding these requires the generated
  contract, Telemetry README, and privacy-review workflow in `AGENTS.md`.
- **Run log:** local `heartbeat_run_events` and measured performance events.
  Useful for correlation, but a local event is not proof of Honeycomb export.

Observability changes within the closed span-attribute allowlist do not need the
Telemetry privacy review. Preserve the endpoint gate and no-operation behavior.

## Find the application's trace

1. Resolve the instance, company, issue, agent, **run UUID**, and UTC interval.
   Record the effective harness/model, workspace/repository, warm or fresh session,
   and actual deployed revision. A task identifier is not a run UUID; one task
   can have several runs, and one run can have several execution attempts.
2. Prefer existing Honeycomb tools when exposed and authorized. Otherwise use
   the signed-in browser. The current project link targets team `paperclip`,
   environment `test`, dataset `paperclip`, and `service.name = paperclip`.
   These are defaults in `ui/src/lib/honeycomb-run-link.ts`, not proof of every
   deployment's destination. Verify the target before comparing data.
3. Open **View in Honeycomb** on the run page when available. It requires
   Paperclip Developer Mode and local implicit board or instance-admin access.
   This link queries existing data. **Re-run with provider trace** is a different
   action: it starts work and is not needed to read Honeycomb.
4. Without the link, calculate the same correlation value locally:

   ```sh
   # Set RUN_ID to the exact saved run UUID first; no trailing newline is hashed.
   node -e 'console.log(require("node:crypto").createHash("sha256").update(process.argv[1]).digest("hex").slice(0, 12))' "$RUN_ID"
   ```

   Filter `paperclip.task.run.run_id` to that 12-character lowercase hash and
   `service.name` to the observed service. Start with the run's absolute time
   window. The product link defaults to the last seven days; widen it for older
   runs. Group `COUNT` by `trace.trace_id` to discover matching traces.
5. The product's root filter is `name in [task.execution_attempt,
   task.provider_session, task.run]`. Use Honeycomb's `in` operator, not an
   invented OR group. Remove the name filter when setup failed or preparation
   spans are missing; older/standalone preparation can have a separate trace ID.
6. Open each relevant trace and its span details. A count-only query/export
   cannot establish span durations, parentage, or causal attribution. Capture
   the trace URL, time window, service/version, and relevant span names/timings.

In recent investigations, `HONEYCOMB_TEST_CONFIG_API_KEY` in the operator's
`~/.secrets` could read metadata but could not query traces. Ingest permission,
metadata access, and query access are different. Verify current capabilities;
when queries are unavailable, use the signed-in UI rather than creating a new
key or upgrading permissions. Read only needed secret fields, never dump the
file, and keep values out of commands, artifacts, repository files, and reports.

## Read the timeline correctly

| Interval | Meaning / next inspection |
| --- | --- |
| Run creation → executor start | Admission/queue delay; check drain, capacity, and dispatch evidence |
| `task.execution_attempt` | Server executor invocation through preparation, dispatch, durable reply, and cleanup |
| `heartbeat.prepare.*`, `native.controller.*` | Controller preparation; expand workspace, configuration, backend, and runtime-selection work |
| `task.provider_session` | Native provider lifecycle; includes preparation and execution, ends before outer workspace persistence |
| `task.run` | Legacy adapter root |
| `runner.session.startup`, `environment.*`, `stage.*`, `sandbox.*` | Runner/environment acquisition, workspace transfer, and startup |
| `agent.turn` | Agent turn time; inspect actual children before calling all of it model latency |
| `execution.workspace_finalize`, `workspace_sync.*`, `completion.*`, `response.*` | Copyback, settlement, response persistence, and publication work |

The attempt and provider lifecycle are linked roots; they need not share a trace
ID. Neither is a guarantee of one continuous trace across queueing or restarts.
Correlate with the run log and saved reply timestamps. The native local event
`task.run.measured` includes terminal elapsed time and durable copyback.

Use start/end times to compare serial intervals and the union of parallel work.
Never add a parent to its children or sum parallel branches as elapsed time.
For example, `configuration_skills` is inside `execution_configuration`, and
`skills.prepare` overlaps the broader `heartbeat.prepare_before_environment`.
Detail spans are capped at 16 per name per attempt; missing per-item children
do not mean later items did no work.

Distinguish first streamed text, committed reply, externally delivered message,
and browser paint. A successful `response.transaction.commit` proves durable storage;
`response.publish` is enqueueing and `execution.realtime` is server dispatch.
Neither proves that the user saw the response. Choose the boundary the user asked
to improve, then measure the whole path to that boundary.

For slow issue pages, combine `issue.read.<phase>` with `Server-Timing`
(`paperclip_issue`, `issue_<phase>`) and the browser's request waterfall and
`issue-detail:navigate→content-paint` measure. Concurrent reads overlap. Fast
API completion does not establish fast conversation reveal or rendering.

A long parent span without children is an attribution gap. It does not prove
SQL, network, or model time. For database hypotheses, use
[fix-slow-queries](../fix-slow-queries/SKILL.md). For CPU hypotheses, use a bounded
authorized profile covering the actual slow phase; a sample taken while queued
cannot explain preparation. Low aggregate container CPU does not exclude a
blocked Node main thread. Keep profiled diagnostics separate from unprofiled
acceptance timings.

## Design a human-readable waterfall

A collapsed trace should tell a person what the system is doing; expanding a
phase should explain where its time went. Before adding or reorganizing spans,
sketch the meaningful phases and compare them with the existing exported tree.
For application runs, make preparation, runner startup, agent work, and settlement
easy to distinguish. For CI, retain workflow/job/step/file/test ownership.

- Group by purpose: file staging belongs under `stage.sync`, with workspace and
  asset branches such as `stage.asset.home`; provider operations belong beneath
  the work that caused them. Reuse the owning path's existing semantic groups.
- Use real OpenTelemetry parent contexts. A dotted name or a `parentName`
  attribute alone does not make a foldable hierarchy. A flat trace can need
  better parentage even when it already has enough measurements.
- Preserve useful detail beneath the groups. Improve folding before deleting
  spans; account for any measurement moved to an attribute, event, or run log.
- Make the hierarchy truthful on failure and during concurrent work. Cleanup
  belongs to settlement even when startup fails; long-lived processes need an
  owner that covers their lifetime. Preserve documented links between separate
  attempts and provider lifecycles rather than forcing everything into one root.

Read [trace design](references/trace-design.md) when designing or reviewing a
hierarchy. It includes a staging example, lifecycle pitfalls, and acceptance
checks for the actual exported waterfall. The current Observability contract
owns exact span names and boundaries; historical examples are not a new schema.

## Add only the missing instrumentation

Read applicable repository rules before editing. Reuse the existing timing seams:

- `server/src/services/execution-preparation-timing.ts`:
  `withRunExecutionTiming`, `createRunPreparationTiming`, `measureRunPhase`, and
  `beginRunPhase`. Use the existing attempt; do not create a new root per detail.
- `server/src/services/native-runtime/native-run-trace.ts`: native lifecycle
  hierarchy and links to the owning attempt.
- `server/src/services/issue-read-timing.ts`: issue-read phases and Server-Timing.
- `packages/adapter-utils/src/acpx-engine/startup-timing.ts`: runtime parent
  context and closed span attributes. Adapter utilities receive the host context
  rather than constructing an independent exporter.

Extend the closed phase union when a meaningful boundary is missing. Wrap the
actual awaited operation, preserve parent context across async/provider boundaries,
and end spans on success and failure. Keep real wall times for spans recorded
after the operation. Use existing hashed IDs, closed enums, and allowed numeric
counts; do not add prompts, tool arguments/results, paths, raw identifiers,
credentials, or exception text. Do not enable all filesystem instrumentation to
explain one slow scan.

Observability must not retry the operation, replace its return/error, change
authorization/locks, or break execution when the tracer fails. Preserve root
sampling and the explicit endpoint gate even if another library registers an
OTel provider. Update `doc/observability.md` when the trace contract changes.
Run focused tests for endpoint-off behavior, parentage/concurrent-run isolation,
failure handling, and the changed seam. Use real exported evidence to claim that
new spans appear in Honeycomb; a unit-test tracer alone does not prove ingestion.
For hierarchy changes, also inspect collapsed and expanded exported views using
the [trace-design acceptance checks](references/trace-design.md#verify-the-exported-waterfall).

## Compare and hand back useful evidence

Choose the largest actionable serial wait or unexplained gap, then reproduce it
at the smallest faithful layer. Compare matched runs: same harness/model,
workspace size, session warmth, concurrency, and relevant revision/configuration.
Report sample count and median/range when several runs are available. Preserve
failures; a failed fast run is not a latency improvement.

Return the run/attempt and trace links, observed revision, end-to-end timing,
dominant non-overlapping phases, uncertainty, and next action or verified gain.
Label local, synthetic, and hosted evidence precisely: a dev-host reproduction
is not a local checkout run, and a merged fix does not prove hosted improvement.
If traces are unavailable, state the missing access or coverage and what the
run log/browser measurements actually establish.

Detail spans are capped at 16 per name per attempt; missing per-item children
do not mean later items did no work.

Distinguish first streamed text, committed reply, externally delivered message,
and browser paint. A successful `response.transaction.commit` proves durable storage;
`response.publish` is enqueueing and `execution.realtime` is server dispatch.
Neither proves that the user saw the response. Choose the boundary the user asked
to improve, then measure the whole path to that boundary.

For slow issue pages, combine `issue.read.<phase>` with `Server-Timing`
(`paperclip_issue`, `issue_<phase>`) and the browser's request waterfall and
`issue-detail:navigate→content-paint` measure. Concurrent reads overlap. Fast
API completion does not establish fast conversation reveal or rendering.

A long parent span without children is an attribution gap. It does not prove
SQL, network, or model time. For database hypotheses, use
[fix-slow-queries](../fix-slow-queries/SKILL.md). For CPU hypotheses, use a bounded
authorized profile covering the actual slow phase; a sample taken while queued
cannot explain preparation. Low aggregate container CPU does not exclude a
blocked Node main thread. Keep profiled diagnostics separate from unprofiled
acceptance timings.

## Design a human-readable waterfall

A collapsed trace should tell a person what the system is doing; expanding a
phase should explain where its time went. Before adding or reorganizing spans,
sketch the meaningful phases and compare them with the existing exported tree.
For application runs, make preparation, runner startup, agent work, and settlement
easy to distinguish. For CI, retain workflow/job/step/file/test ownership.

- Group by purpose: file staging belongs under `stage.sync`, with workspace and
  asset branches such as `stage.asset.home`; provider operations belong beneath
  the work that caused them. Reuse the owning path's existing semantic groups.
- Use real OpenTelemetry parent contexts. A dotted name or a `parentName`
  attribute alone does not make a foldable hierarchy. A flat trace can need
  better parentage even when it already has enough measurements.
- Preserve useful detail beneath the groups. Improve folding before deleting
  spans; account for any measurement moved to an attribute, event, or run log.
- Make the hierarchy truthful on failure and during concurrent work. Cleanup
  belongs to settlement even when startup fails; long-lived processes need an
  owner that covers their lifetime. Preserve documented links between separate
  attempts and provider lifecycles rather than forcing everything into one root.

Read [trace design](references/trace-design.md) when designing or reviewing a
hierarchy. It includes a staging example, lifecycle pitfalls, and acceptance
checks for the actual exported waterfall. The current Observability contract
owns exact span names and boundaries; historical examples are not a new schema.

## Add only the missing instrumentation

Read applicable repository rules before editing. Reuse the existing timing seams:

- `server/src/services/execution-preparation-timing.ts`:
  `withRunExecutionTiming`, `createRunPreparationTiming`, `measureRunPhase`, and
  `beginRunPhase`. Use the existing attempt; do not create a new root per detail.
- `server/src/services/native-runtime/native-run-trace.ts`: native lifecycle
  hierarchy and links to the owning attempt.
- `server/src/services/issue-read-timing.ts`: issue-read phases and Server-Timing.
- `packages/adapter-utils/src/acpx-engine/startup-timing.ts`: runtime parent
  context and closed span attributes. Adapter utilities receive the host context
  rather than constructing an independent exporter.

Extend the closed phase union when a meaningful boundary is missing. Wrap the
actual awaited operation, preserve parent context across async/provider boundaries,
and end spans on success and failure. Keep real wall times for spans recorded
after the operation. Use existing hashed IDs, closed enums, and allowed numeric
counts; do not add prompts, tool arguments/results, paths, raw identifiers,
credentials, or exception text. Do not enable all filesystem instrumentation to
explain one slow scan.

Observability must not retry the operation, replace its return/error, change
authorization/locks, or break execution when the tracer fails. Preserve root
sampling and the explicit endpoint gate even if another library registers an
OTel provider. Update `doc/observability.md` when the trace contract changes.
Run focused tests for endpoint-off behavior, parentage/concurrent-run isolation,
failure handling, and the changed seam. Use real exported evidence to claim that
new spans appear in Honeycomb; a unit-test tracer alone does not prove ingestion.
For hierarchy changes, also inspect collapsed and expanded exported views using
the [trace-design acceptance checks](references/trace-design.md#verify-the-exported-waterfall).

## Compare and hand back useful evidence

Choose the largest actionable serial wait or unexplained gap, then reproduce it
at the smallest faithful layer. Compare matched runs: same harness/model,
workspace size, session warmth, concurrency, and relevant revision/configuration.
Report sample count and median/range when several runs are available. Preserve
failures; a failed fast run is not a latency improvement.

Return the run/attempt and trace links, observed revision, end-to-end timing,
dominant non-overlapping phases, uncertainty, and next action or verified gain.
Label local, synthetic, and hosted evidence precisely: a dev-host reproduction
is not a local checkout run, and a merged fix does not prove hosted improvement.
If traces are unavailable, state the missing access or coverage and what the
run log/browser measurements actually establish.

skills.name: maintain-storybook
skills.desc: Keep Paperclip stories and their downstream catalog aligned with the feature map and production UI. Use to reconcile story drift, classify prototypes, update fixtures, or maintain feature coverage.
skills.body:
---
name: maintain-storybook
description: Keep Paperclip stories and their downstream catalog aligned with the feature map and production UI. Use to reconcile story drift, classify prototypes, update fixtures, or maintain feature coverage.
---

# Maintain Storybook

Read the [Storybook catalog contract](../../../maps/storybook-map/README.md),
the relevant [feature recipes](../../../maps/feature-map/README.md), and
[DESIGN.md](../../../DESIGN.md). The feature map is an upstream input. This skill
owns stories, their fixtures/support, and `maps/storybook-map/`; it does not edit
the feature or agent-access maps. Report upstream drift to
`maintain-verification-skill` with source evidence.

## Reconcile the requested scope

For a feature/change, follow its capability IDs to catalog entries and shared
dependencies. For a full inventory, account for every configured story file,
including historical examples. Start with `node scripts/storybook-catalog.mjs`.
Record the source revision and whether the pass covers source, rendering,
interactions, or visual comparisons. Inventory completeness is not behavioral
coverage. Do not expand a targeted maintenance request into an all-product audit.

Compare each affected story's rendered subject, props, fixture responses, actions,
and assertions with the production implementation and recipe. Follow imported
wrappers: a production Button inside a locally recreated page does not make that
page a production-component story. A real production page using mocked APIs is
valid isolation; record component provenance and data simulation separately.
Inspect mock methods/paths, payload shapes, errors, identity, gates, and reset
behavior. An API method returning success without the relevant state transition
can hide drift. Do not replace errors with generic successful mocks to pass.

Prefer mounting the shipped subject and mocking its external boundary. Retain
local layout wrappers and fixture data when they serve that isolation. Replace a
duplicate product implementation only when the current component expresses the
same scenario without losing the original purpose. Production bugs and larger
redesigns are separate findings, not reasons to rewrite expected behavior.

Classify current examples, proposals, historical explorations, and unresolved
cases explicitly. Use `unreviewed` when evidence does not establish parity.
Retain useful superseded work with its rationale and replacement reference;
do not delete a story merely because it is old, mocked, or duplicated by name.
Record mixed suites honestly and split them only when that improves review.

## Preserve identity and keep the index useful

Assign existing stable `area/capability` references, with one primary reference
and optional related references. Foundations and unmapped proposals need explicit
reasons rather than invented capabilities. Cross-cutting stories have one source
and several references. Do not count historical/proposed stories as current
feature coverage.

For shared foundations that demonstrate a mapped capability, keep their existing
folder/sidebar with `home: "foundations"` and an exception reason, then add related
capability references. Inspect the named exports before linking them. Notes must
name the demonstrated states and remaining limits; an association does not certify
the whole capability. If a story reveals a shipped capability absent upstream,
reconcile its feature recipe and access companion through map maintenance first.

Preserve story exports and IDs. Before moves/title changes, capture the existing
built `index.json`; use explicit meta IDs when needed and compare IDs afterward.
Place stories under `ui/storybook/stories/<primary-feature-area>/`. Use the feature
map's section and feature names as their sidebar prefix; keep useful scenario
groupings beneath that prefix. Put shared fixture modules in `ui/storybook/support/`.
Keep the explicit CSF meta ID stable even when the title changes; the generated
catalog derives `stableId` from it. Unmapped component examples belong under Foundations; the catalog guide
belongs under Overview. The checker verifies these conventions.

Keep the main guide and every feature Overview congruent with the upstream index:
same section/feature names and order, all capabilities in recipe order, related
suite links across primary homes, and explicit missing examples. Run `node scripts/storybook-catalog.mjs` to regenerate ignored indexes, feature
pages, and preview ordering. Storybook startup/build also generates them. Never
hand-edit or commit generated output. Generated guides are not example coverage.
Preserve their `feature-map-<area>--overview` IDs. The generator removes obsolete
pages from its own ignored output directory when areas disappear.

Keep review links and snapshot names working. Prefer classification fixes before
bulk directory moves. Store capability associations, classification, and durable
limits in each story's literal `parameters.paperclip` object. Infer file paths,
exports and stable IDs from CSF; do not maintain a second inventory. Use Git diff
and history to choose changed production subjects, fixtures and shared sources
for review. Record source revision and executed evidence in the PR or CI report;
do not refresh hashes, dates, or a shared review journal.

Verification routes belong in each feature recipe's optional `Storybook
verification` section. Report needed corrections to `maintain-verification-skill`.
Distinguish missing shipped UI examples from CLI/operator operations and real
browser checks. Keep concrete production contracts and existing test starting
points; test presence is not passing evidence. The generated verification report
lists capabilities without current examples. Associating an example must not
discard its separate production verification obligations.

Run `node scripts/storybook-catalog.mjs --check` and
`node --test scripts/check-maps.test.mjs scripts/storybook-catalog.test.mjs scripts/storybook-feature-index.test.mjs`.
Checks validate local annotations, discovered inventory and references, not
semantic parity or runtime health.
Use `review-storybook` for affected rendering and interactions. Reuse the existing
Storybook/Playwright tools; add no separate launcher, runtime, or baseline system.
Do not accept new screenshot baselines as part of a catalog cleanup.

Report what was corrected, retained, and still needs review, naming exact files
and capabilities. Keep source-only results separate from executed results and
name blocked checks. A full pass must not hide unreviewed stories or claim that
fixture interactions establish production API, permission, or provider behavior.

skills.name: maintain-verification-skill
skills.desc: Keep a project's verification skill and product/agent access maps aligned with current source and real evidence. Use for /maintain-verification-skill, auditing the verify skill, or reconciling feature and agent access coverage.
skills.body:
---
name: maintain-verification-skill
description: "Keep a project's verification skill and product/agent access maps aligned with current source and real evidence. Use for /maintain-verification-skill, auditing the verify skill, or reconciling feature and agent access coverage."
---

# Maintain a verification skill and its maps

Keep user journeys and agent access aligned with the app. For Paperclip, read the
[map contract](../../../maps/README.md), the
[feature index](../../../maps/feature-map/README.md), and the
[agent access index](../../../maps/agent-access-map/README.md). These are sibling
maps under `maps/`, with the same area filenames and capability IDs. Preserve
[Poteto's product format](../create-verification-skill/references/feature-map-example/).
Agent companions follow the shared contract; they do not duplicate user recipes.

An API endpoint, an OpenAPI actor label, a declared scenario tool and an admitted
production agent path are different evidence. Verify which permitted agent
surface can actually express an operation. Track source review, operation review
and executed proof separately. A source-only baseline is useful, but cannot
certify complete coverage or live behavior.

## Outcomes

Pick one and report source scope, live scope and remaining gaps separately:

- **clean** — the requested scope got source and live coverage, with no corrections.
- **changed** — proven skill/map/check corrections are ready to review; name any
  access gaps or unexecuted coverage that remains.
- **blocked** — requested coverage or a proven correction could not finish; name
  the unmet prerequisite and evidence captured so far.

A targeted audit covers its named areas; do not present it as a full pass. A full
pass reads every area from source and exercises every reachable feature, plus
relevant permitted-agent and denial paths. Report unreachable prerequisites and
not-run operations rather than silently reducing the scope.

## Edit scope

For Paperclip, edit the target verification skill, these maintenance instructions
when needed, `maps/`, and the map-specific structural check
`scripts/check-maps.mjs` / `scripts/check-maps.test.mjs`. Fix references to those
maps in contributor docs or skill instructions when their locations/IDs change.
Keep the maps in `maps/{feature-map,agent-access-map}/`, outside skill directories.

For other projects, maintain their existing verification skill and map locations;
the Paperclip directory convention does not authorize relocating another repo.
Never edit product APIs, permission enforcement, tool bindings or UI behavior
in a maintenance run. Record product/access gaps for implementation separately;
a permission denial is not authorization to widen access.

## Pass

0. **Locate the target and scope.** Find the project-local verification skill
   (usually `.agents/skills/verify-*/`). Several candidates: ask which; none:
   point to `/create-verification-skill`. Honor a requested narrower audit.
   Use Git diff/history to identify affected sources. Record the source revision
   and review evidence in the PR or evidence report, not a shared map ledger.

1. **Check both indexes.** Pair same-named feature and agent files, then match
   stable sub-feature IDs. Fix orphan/missing entries and broken references.
   For Paperclip run `node scripts/check-maps.mjs`. This checks structure,
   not API authorization, real tool bindings or live behavior.

2. **Source wave.** Use read-only subagents per area, with each reader owning
   the feature file and its access companion; schedule within available slots.
   Readers never edit or drive the app. Each returns the user capability/source
   entry points, likely drift with citations, meaningful operations, their APIs,
   actor/grant/resource/run/mode boundaries, real agent entry points by surface,
   missing access/discovery/policy decisions, and a concise verification recipe.
   Follow recent changes to routes, contracts, authorization, native tool
   admission, CLI and MCP as well as UI. Inspect actual route/service policy;
   compare it with OpenAPI and production bindings, not only scenario catalogs.

3. **Reconcile both maps.** Spot-check cited drift and merge recipes into as
   few app states as practical. Every affected business operation needs an API
   and a permitted agent path, or an explicit gap. A dedicated tool is optional
   when existing API/CLI/MCP fallback suffices. Distinguish native/remote access
   from legacy REST and personal assistant OAuth. Record field/scope limits,
   unavailable clients, protocol requirements and native fallback restrictions.
   Keep justified local/developer/operator exceptions, but split shared data
   operations from presentation. A board-only route records a restriction and
   any existing request/result handoff; an unresolved delegation question stays
   visible. Split broad baselines into per-operation records before marking
   them operation-reviewed. Add newly discovered capabilities only with concrete
   source; add their companion at the same time. Each feature recipe carries its
   own navigation metadata. Discovery generates the feature and access indexes;
   do not register new areas in shared READMEs or commit generated output. Keep
   durable Storybook verification routes in the affected feature recipe.

4. **Live pass.** Required for a verification maintenance pass even if source
   looks clean. The coordinator owns serial driving, using the target skill's
   existing launch/doctor/evidence/cleanup workflow and Paperclip's existing
   API/runner/MCP fixtures. Exercise the real user path and the relevant actual
   agent path separately. For access checks use the permitted agent identity,
   run, mode and target; assert results and relevant denials. A board request or
   board test-as-agent does not replace agent-credential proof. Use disposable
   fixtures for mutation/denial tests and record simulated providers honestly.
   Never assume an optional client is admitted to a native run.

   Keep three invariants: health-check before driving and after surprises;
   verify captured evidence survives cleanup; clean up everything the drive
   owned once no longer needed. Reset a wedged UI even if process health passes.
   Follow the target skill's session model: one long-lived owned server/UI
   instance, or isolated short-lived CLI sessions. After a skill-induced failure,
   fix within edit scope and retry once, restarting only what was invalidated.
   Record missing auth/provider/environment prerequisites and attempted paths.
   Re-drive changed harness helpers before shipping them. Final teardown follows
   the last proof attempt and preserves evidence.

5. **Triage and record.** User description/recipe drift updates the product map;
   endpoint/path/permission/discovery drift updates its companion. Missing or
   broken product behavior stays a product gap, with evidence. Never rewrite a
   recipe or mark an access exception to bless a failure. Map evidence states
   remain source-only/not-run unless an actual proof supports the named operation
   and surface. Keep run artifacts/results in the evidence location or issue;
   the generated `maps/generated/coverage.json` is a page-reference inventory,
   not passing test evidence.

6. **Review corrections.** Re-read changed files, check paired IDs/references and
   run the smallest relevant validation. Report outcome and source/live coverage
   honestly. If shipping is requested or already authorized, update the existing
   task PR where appropriate, or create at most one PR of proven corrections.
   A clean pass needs no branch or PR. Do not implement access-policy changes
   merely to make the maintenance report green.

Keep concise run notes and proof artifacts in the target skill's named evidence
location; do not commit ephemeral run logs as map content.

Origin and license: [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md).

skills.desc: Create and develop external Paperclip plugins with the CLI-first workflow. Use when scaffolding a plugin, iterating on a local plugin, installing it into Paperclip, or updating plugin authoring docs.
skills.body:
---
name: paperclip-create-plugin
description: >
  Create and develop external Paperclip plugins with the CLI-first workflow. Use
  when scaffolding a plugin, iterating on a local plugin, installing it into
  Paperclip, or updating plugin authoring docs.
---

# Create and develop a Paperclip plugin

Use this skill when the task is to create, scaffold, or iterate on a Paperclip plugin against a local Paperclip instance.

## 1. Default: build the plugin OUTSIDE Paperclip core

Plugins are their own packages. Unless the task **explicitly** asks for a bundled in-repo example, do not add plugin source under `packages/plugins/` in this repo.

- Scaffold the plugin into a directory outside the Paperclip checkout (e.g. `~/dev/paperclip-plugins/<name>`).
- Install it into the running Paperclip instance by local absolute path.
- Edit code in the external package; let Paperclip pick up rebuilt output.

Only edit Paperclip core itself when the user asks to surface a plugin as a bundled example (`server/src/routes/plugins.ts`, in-repo example lists, docs).

## 2. Ground rules

Reference docs when you need detail:

1. `doc/plugins/PLUGIN_AUTHORING_GUIDE.md`
2. `packages/plugins/sdk/README.md`
3. `doc/plugins/PLUGIN_SPEC.md` — future-looking context only

Current runtime assumptions:

- plugin workers are trusted code
- plugin UI is trusted same-origin host code
- worker APIs are capability-gated
- plugin UI is not sandboxed by manifest capabilities
- no host-provided shared plugin UI component kit yet
- `ctx.assets` is not supported in the current runtime

## 3. CLI-first scaffold workflow

Use `paperclipai plugin init`. Do not invoke the scaffold package node entrypoint by hand unless the CLI command is unavailable in the environment.

```bash
paperclipai plugin init @acme/my-plugin --output ~/dev/paperclip-plugins
```

Useful flags (all optional):

- `--output <dir>` — parent directory; the command creates `<dir>/<unscoped-name>/`. Defaults to the current directory.
- `--template <default|connector|workspace|environment>` — starter template.
- `--category <connector|workspace|automation|ui|environment>` — manifest category.
- `--display-name <name>`, `--description <text>`, `--author <name>` — manifest metadata.
- `--sdk-path <path>` — snapshot the local SDK from a Paperclip checkout into `.paperclip-sdk/` (useful when developing against an unreleased SDK).

On success the command prints the exact next commands (`cd`, `pnpm install`, `pnpm dev`, `paperclipai plugin install <abs-path>`). Run them in order.

If `paperclipai` is not on PATH in your environment, fall back to:

```bash
pnpm --filter @paperclipai/create-paperclip-plugin build
node packages/plugins/create-paperclip-plugin/dist/index.js @acme/my-plugin \
  --output /absolute/path \
  --sdk-path /absolute/path/to/paperclip/packages/plugins/sdk
```

## 4. Local install + rebuild loop

In the scaffolded plugin folder:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev            # esbuild --watch: rebuilds dist/manifest.js, dist/worker.js, dist/ui/
paperclipai plugin install /absolute/path/to/my-plugin
```

Notes:

- `paperclipai plugin install` auto-detects local paths (absolute, `./`, `../`, `~`, or an existing relative folder) and forwards `isLocalPath: true` to the server. Pass `--local` to force local mode if the heuristic is ambiguous.
- Paths are resolved to absolute paths before being sent to the server.
- The server watches built outputs (`dist/`) for local-path plugins and restarts the plugin worker on rebuild — you do not need to reinstall after every edit.
- UI hot reload via the SDK dev server (`pnpm dev:ui`, port `4177`) is optional and template-dependent; only mention it if the template wires `devUiUrl` and you verified it works end to end.
- `--version` only applies to npm package installs. Combining it with a local path is an error.

After install, inspect with:

```bash
paperclipai plugin list
paperclipai plugin inspect <plugin-key>
```

## 5. After scaffolding, sanity-check the package

Open and confirm:

- `src/manifest.ts` — declared capabilities and slots
- `src/worker.ts` — worker entry
- `src/ui/index.tsx` — UI entry (if applicable)
- `tests/plugin.spec.ts` — placeholder test
- `package.json` — `paperclipPlugin` block points at `dist/manifest.js`, `dist/worker.js`, `dist/ui/`

Make sure the plugin:

- declares only supported capabilities
- does not use `ctx.assets`
- does not import host UI component stubs
- keeps UI self-contained
- uses `routePath` only on `page` slots

## 6. Verification (run before declaring success)

From the plugin folder:

```bash
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
pnpm build
```

If the plugin is already running under `pnpm dev`, you can keep the watcher up and run `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm test` in a separate shell.

If you changed Paperclip SDK/host/plugin runtime code in addition to the plugin, also run the relevant Paperclip workspace checks.

## 7. Success checklist (report this back)

When you finish a local plugin task, report:

- **Scaffold path** — absolute path of the created plugin folder.
- **Commands run** — the exact `paperclipai plugin init`, `pnpm install`, `pnpm dev`, `paperclipai plugin install <path>` invocations (and any verification commands).
- **Install status** — output of `paperclipai plugin list` / `plugin inspect` (plugin key, version, status). Note if `status` is anything other than `ready` and include `lastError`.
- **Tests / build result** — `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`, `pnpm build` pass/fail with the failing output if any.
- **Reload limitations** — call out anything that did not hot-reload (e.g. manifest changes required a reinstall, UI dev server was not wired, etc.).

If any item is missing, mark it as such — do not silently skip.

## 8. When NOT to edit Paperclip core

Do not add the plugin under `packages/plugins/` or update bundled-example wiring unless the user explicitly asks for a bundled example. Local-path installs are the supported development model; npm packages are the production deployment path.

If the user does ask for a bundled example, also update:

- `server/src/routes/plugins.ts` example list
- any docs that enumerate in-repo example plugins

## 9. Documentation expectations

When authoring or updating plugin docs:

- distinguish current implementation from future spec ideas
- be explicit about the trusted-code model
- do not promise host UI components or asset APIs
- prefer local-path development + npm-package deployment guidance over repo-local workflows
